doan.chu: Located in Vietnam’s northwestern highlands, Lào Cai is characterized by towering mountain ranges, deep valleys, and winding terraced rice fields stretching through the clouds.

It is home to diverse ethnic communities, including the H’Mông, Dao, Tày, Giáy, Hà Nhì, and Xa Phó, each contributing to a rich cultural landscape through vibrant traditional clothing, highland markets, folk dances, khèn music, and distinctive festivals.
Lào Cai is also renowned for tea cultivation and processing, particularly ancient Shan Tuyết tea, as well as local specialties that capture the flavors of the mountains and forests.

Mountain weather and road conditions can change quickly. Check the local forecast, confirm transportation with your accommodation, and leave extra time between destinations rather than planning your trip too tightly.

Ask Before Taking Photos: People, homes, ceremonies, and traditional clothing are not tourist props. Always ask before taking close-up photographs, particularly of elders, children, or private activities.
Don't Enter Homes Without Permission: If you are invited into a local home, follow your host's guidance. Customs may differ between communities, so when in doubt, ask rather than assume.
Dress for the Setting: When visiting homes, places of worship, or participating in community events, wear clothing appropriate to the environment and follow local guidance.

Don't Treat Culture as a Performance: Traditional clothing, farming, cooking, rituals, and daily work are part of people's lives. Avoid asking people to repeat an activity simply for a photograph or video.

Support, Don't Exploit: Whenever possible, buy directly from local producers, stay at locally owned accommodations, and pay fairly for services. Avoid giving money or gifts to children as a tourist activity; if you want to contribute, consider supporting community-led initiatives instead.

When in Doubt, Ask: A respectful question is always better than an assumption. Your host, guide, or local business owner will often be the best person to explain what is appropriate in their community

Located in northern Vietnam, Bắc Ninh is a culturally rich region of the Kinh Bắc area, shaped by rivers, fertile plains, traditional villages, and historic settlements.

Located in north-central Vietnam, Nghệ An stretches from the coast to the mountains of the western border, creating a diverse landscape of beaches, forests, rivers, valleys, and highland villages.

The province is home to diverse communities, including the Thái, Thổ, Khơ Mú, Ơ Đu, H’Mông, and Kinh. Their cultural heritage remains visible through traditional stilt houses, brocade weaving, folk music, festivals, local cuisine, and community life. Western Nghệ An is also part of the Pù Mát World Biosphere Reserve, combining rich biodiversity with the cultural heritage of mountain communities.

Nghệ An is also known for its historical and cultural sites, including Kim Liên, the hometown of President Ho Chi Minh, alongside its beaches, national parks, waterfalls, and traditional craft villages.

Located in south-central Vietnam, Khánh Hòa stretches from the coast and islands to mountains and highland communities, creating a diverse landscape of beaches, bays, islands, forests, salt fields, and rural villages.

The province is home to diverse communities, including the Chăm, Raglai, and Kinh. Their cultural heritage remains visible through traditional pottery, brocade weaving, gong music, festivals, fishing traditions, salt-making, local cuisine, and community life.

Located at the southernmost tip of Vietnam, Cà Mau is a land of rivers, canals, mangrove forests, wetlands, and coastal ecosystems. Its landscapes are shaped by the meeting of freshwater and saltwater, creating a distinctive way of life closely connected to the sea, forests, and waterways.

Cà Mau is home to a rich river-and-coastal culture, where local livelihoods have long revolved around fishing, shrimp farming, crab harvesting, agriculture, and forest resources.     Community-based tourism allows visitors to experience this everyday life while supporting locally owned households and protecting fragile ecosystems.
The province is also home to Mũi Cà Mau National Park and U Minh Hạ National Park, both part of the Mũi Cà Mau World Biosphere Reserve.

doan.chu: Check the weather before boat trips and forest activities. Confirm transportation and community-tourism arrangements with your host in advance.
Fishing boats, homes, farms, and people's daily work are private spaces. Ask before taking close-up photographs.
Shrimp farming, fishing, crab catching, and forest work are people's livelihoods—not staged tourist activities.
Don't Enter Private Areas Without Permission:
Ask before entering homes, shrimp ponds, fishing areas, or family-run businesses.
Stay on designated routes and avoid damaging roots, plants, mudflats, or wildlife habitats.
Stay with local families, eat at locally owned businesses, and purchase directly from local producers where possible.
Take your waste with you, especially when traveling by boat or visiting remote wetlands.
Local hosts and community-tourism operators can explain what is appropriate in their area.

Cà Mau's traditional industries are closely tied to its natural environment, particularly shrimp, fish, rice, mangrove forests, and waterways. The province currently has 10 recognized craft villages, while local authorities are increasingly connecting traditional products with OCOP and sustainable tourism.
